q: Unless their agreement provides otherwise, a principal who hires an agent for pay owes the agent all of the following duties EXCEPT:
choices: A duty to pay the agent the agreed compensation for the agent's services
A duty to reimburse the agent for expenses, and indemnify the agent for losses, that the agent reasonably incurs while acting within the agent's authority
A duty to cooperate with the agent and not to interfere with the agent's performance of the agency
A fiduciary duty of loyalty that requires the principal to put the agent's interests ahead of the principal's own
explain: The duties a principal owes an agent are compensation, reimbursement and indemnification for authorized acts, and cooperation, and they arise from the agency agreement and the principal's role rather than from a fiduciary relationship. The fiduciary duties of loyalty, obedience and care run the other way, from the agent to the principal. The reimbursement and indemnification choice is a real duty, but it covers only expenses and losses incurred within the agent's authority, not losses the agent causes by acting outside it.
source: Cornell LII Wex, principal; Cornell LII Wex, fiduciary duty (agent's duties run to the principal). Principal's duties to the agent NOT confirmed from a fetched source

q: Lena, acting within her actual authority, contracts to buy a warehouse from Seller. She tells Seller that she is buying for a client who wishes to remain anonymous and signs the contract "Lena, as agent." Seller and Lena never agree that Lena will not be a party to the contract. The client later refuses to close. Whom may Seller hold liable on the contract?
choices: Only the client, because Seller knew that Lena was acting for a principal
Only Lena, because a principal whose identity is not disclosed cannot be bound
Both the client and Lena
Neither, because Seller agreed to contract with an unnamed party
explain: The client is a partially disclosed principal: Seller knew that Lena acted for a principal but did not know who it was. The principal is bound by a contract its agent makes within actual authority, and because Seller could not look to an unknown principal, the agent is also a party to the contract unless the agent and the third party agree otherwise. The choice naming only the client states the rule for a fully disclosed principal, where the third party knows both that there is a principal and who it is.
source: Cornell LII Wex, undisclosed principal (principal bound by acts within actual authority). Agent's liability for a partially disclosed principal NOT confirmed from a fetched source

q: Mark is the purchasing agent of Ridge Co. He signs two contracts "Ridge Co., by Mark, purchasing agent." The first, with Supplier A, is within his actual authority. The second, with Supplier B, is outside any actual or apparent authority he has, and Supplier B does not know that. Mark gave no disclaimer of his authority, and Ridge Co. refuses to ratify the second contract. Which statement is correct?
choices: Mark is liable on both contracts, because he signed both of them
Mark is not liable on either contract, because he disclosed his principal on both
Mark is not a party to the contract with Supplier A, but he is liable to Supplier B for breach of the implied warranty of authority
Mark is liable to Supplier A as a co-party, but he is not liable to Supplier B, because the contract with Supplier B does not bind anyone
explain: An agent who makes an authorized contract for a disclosed principal is not a party to it, so only Ridge Co. is bound to Supplier A. An agent who purports to act for a principal impliedly warrants that he has authority, so when Mark acted without authority and Ridge Co. did not ratify, Mark is liable to Supplier B for breach of that warranty. Disclosing the principal protects the agent only when he actually has the authority he claims.
source: Cornell LII Wex, agency; Cornell LII Wex, actual authority; Cornell LII Wex, apparent authority. Agent's nonliability on an authorized contract for a disclosed principal and the implied warranty of authority NOT confirmed from a fetched source

q: Before Lark Corp. was incorporated, its promoter, Dana, signed a contract with Vendor to buy equipment for the corporation. The contract says nothing about Dana's personal liability. After Lark was incorporated, its board formally adopted the contract. Vendor never agreed to release Dana. Lark later fails to pay. Whom may Vendor hold liable?
choices: Only Lark, because the adoption substituted Lark for Dana
Only Dana, because a corporation cannot be bound by a contract made before it existed
Both Lark and Dana, because adoption binds the corporation but does not release the promoter
Neither, because the contract was made for a corporation that did not exist when it was signed
explain: A promoter who signs a contract for a corporation not yet formed is personally liable on it, and the corporation becomes bound only if it adopts the contract after it is formed. Adoption adds the corporation as a party but does not release the promoter. Only a novation, in which the other party agrees to substitute the corporation and release the promoter, ends the promoter's liability, and Vendor never agreed to one.
source: Cornell LII Wex, promoter (promoter's acts taken over by the board after incorporation); Cornell LII Wex, novation (release requires agreement of both original parties). Promoter's continuing liability after adoption NOT confirmed from a fetched source

q: Ava has owned 2% of the voting shares of Birch Corp. for three years. Birch is incorporated in a state that has adopted the Model Business Corporation Act (MBCA) records-inspection provisions. She suspects that the officers are mismanaging inventory and wants to inspect Birch's accounting records for inventory. Which statement about her right to inspect is correct?
choices: She may inspect them only after obtaining a court order, because accounting records are confidential

She may inspect them if she gives advance written demand made in good faith and for a proper purpose, describes the purpose and the records with reasonable particularity, and the records are directly connected with that purpose
She may not inspect them, because a shareholder must own at least 5% of the shares to inspect accounting records
She may inspect any of Birch's records at any time during business hours without giving notice or stating a purpose
explain: Accounting records are open to a shareholder who gives advance written demand made in good faith and for a proper purpose, describes the purpose and the records with reasonable particularity, and asks only for records directly connected with that purpose; checking for suspected mismanagement is a proper purpose. Her 2% stake does not bar her: even an adopting state that adds a holding test, such as Virginia, also admits anyone who has held shares for six months. No court order is needed; a court steps in only if the corporation refuses a proper demand.
source: Va. Code 13.1-770 E, 13.1-771 A, C and D, and 13.1-773 B (Virginia's adoption of the MBCA records-inspection sections), law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title13.1/chapter9/section13.1-771/
